passages.happening:
“Now there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you. They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them—bringing swift destruction on themselves” (verse 1).

“Many will follow in their depravity, and because of them the way of truth will be defamed. In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words. The longstanding verdict against them remains in force, and their destruction does not sleep” (verses 2-3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 1 ended with the true prophets, who spoke from God. Chapter 2 begins with the false ones. Israel had false prophets, and the church will have false teachers.

Notice where they come from: ‘among you’. The danger is not only from outside. It is from people inside the church, who speak its language and sit at its meals (verse 13). They work ‘secretly’, slipping their teaching in beside the truth.

What do they do? They deny ‘the Master who bought them’. ‘Master’ is the word for a slave's owner. Christ bought his people, as a slave is bought by a new owner, and these teachers rebel against the one who owns them by right. They live in ‘depravity’, and others follow them, so that outsiders sneer at ‘the way of truth’. And they are greedy. They ‘exploit you with deceptive words’, using smooth talk to get money.

Peter's word for them is hard. Their judgment is not asleep, even if it seems slow. That will matter in chapter 3, when people mock the slowness of God.

These fierce words are not for every person a believer disagrees with. They are for teachers who deny Christ, live without restraint, and exploit people for gain. And their aim is to protect those such teachers prey on.
passages.ot:
The law warned Israel against false prophets, even ones who performed signs: “you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer. For the LORD your God is testing you to find out whether you love Him with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 13:3).

Jeremiah said of the false prophets of his day, “The prophets are prophesying lies in My name,” and, “I did not send them or appoint them or speak to them” (Jeremiah 14:14).

And Ezekiel spoke against shepherds who fed on the flock: “For I will deliver My flock from their mouths, and it will no longer be food for them” (Ezekiel 34:10).
passages.hard:
Verse 1 says the false teachers deny ‘the Master who bought them’. Did Christ buy even those who end up denying him?

Christians answer this in different ways, and these notes do not choose. Those who hold that Christ died for all people see in this verse clear evidence that he bought even those who deny him. Those who hold to particular redemption, that Christ died effectively for those God chose, suggest that Peter describes the teachers as they presented themselves, or uses the language of ownership broadly, of Christ's rightful claim over all who have professed his name.

Both agree on the pastoral point. To deny the Lord who paid for you is a terrible thing, and the warning is meant to be heeded, not only debated.

And a word to anyone who has been exploited by a teacher like these. If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith; the Corinthians were taken in too. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whom you listen to, and what they want from you. Ask whether a teacher you admire points you to Christ as Master, or to himself. And ask what it means for you that you were bought.

passages.happening:
“For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment; if He did not spare the ancient world when He brought the flood on its ungodly people, but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, among the eight; if He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly; and if He rescued Lot, a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless (for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard)” (verses 4-8). And so, “if all this is so, then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment” (verse 9).

“Such punishment is specially reserved for those who indulge the corrupt desires of the flesh and despise authority. Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
In Greek, verses 4 to 10 are one long sentence built on ‘if ... if ... if ... then’. Three times God judged; twice he rescued. So the Lord knows how to do both.

First, ‘the angels when they sinned’. The words ‘cast them deep into hell’ translate one Greek word, tartaroō, ‘to cast into Tartarus’. In Greek stories Tartarus was the deepest pit of the underworld, lower than Hades, where rebels against the gods were imprisoned. Jewish writers of the time also used the word for the place where rebellious angels were held. Peter uses a word his readers knew. He most likely means the beings of Genesis 6:1-4, as Jewish tradition read that passage. The word speaks of being held for judgment, not of the final state.

Second, the flood. God did not spare the world of that time, but he kept Noah and seven others. Genesis records no sermon of Noah's, but Peter calls him ‘a preacher of righteousness’.

Third, Sodom and Gomorrah, reduced to ashes. But God rescued Lot. Peter calls Lot ‘righteous’ and says he was ‘tormented’ by what he saw around him every day. Genesis shows a hesitant man, rescued by the hand of mercy. Peter's point is that God knows his own and brings them out.

That is the comfort hidden in the warning. Each judgment is paired with a rescue. Readers surrounded by false teaching are not forgotten. ‘The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials.’

Then Peter turns back to the teachers: self-indulgent, scornful of authority, so bold they ‘slander glorious beings’, something, Peter says, not even angels dare to do (verse 11).
passages.ot:
Peter draws all three examples from Genesis, which tells how “the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose” (Genesis 6:2). “Then the LORD said to Noah, ‘Go into the ark, you and all your family, because I have found you righteous in this generation’” (Genesis 7:1). “Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah” (Genesis 19:24). And Lot was rescued: “when Lot hesitated, the men grabbed his hand and the hands of his wife and his two daughters. And they led them safely out of the city, because of the LORD’s compassion for them” (Genesis 19:16).

Jesus used the same two examples to warn people to be ready: “Just as it was in the days of Noah, so also will it be in the days of the Son of Man” (Luke 17:26), and “It was the same in the days of Lot” (Luke 17:28).
passages.hard:
Who are the angels who sinned? Does Peter take this from writings outside the Bible? And what about the flood?

Most readers think Peter means the ‘sons of God’ of Genesis 6:1-4, as that passage was read in Jewish tradition: in the book of 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing widely read in the first century, these sons of God were rebellious angels who were imprisoned. Others read Genesis 6 differently, as the family of Seth or as powerful kings, as the notes on Genesis 6 set out, and so take 2 Peter 2:4 more generally, of angels who rebelled. These notes do not choose.

This passage is very close to the short letter of Jude (Jude 6-7), which names 1 Enoch directly elsewhere (Jude 14-15). Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude and left out its direct use of writings outside the Old Testament. Others think Jude used 2 Peter, or that both drew on a common source. Either way, using a word or a picture that readers knew does not make every part of an outside book Scripture.

Peter uses the flood to show that God has judged before and rescued before. These notes take no position on how widely the flood's waters spread or on the age of the earth. Christians who share the same faith differ on those questions, and Peter's point does not depend on them.
passages.asks: Ask whether you have believed that God sees what is happening around you. Ask where you feel, like Lot, worn down by what you see and hear every day. And ask whether you trust that the Lord knows how to rescue you.

passages.happening:
“Yet not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges against them before the Lord. These men are like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be captured and destroyed. They blaspheme in matters they do not understand, and like such creatures, they too will be destroyed” (verses 11-12).

“The harm they will suffer is the wages of their wickedness. They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you. Their eyes are full of adultery; their desire for sin is never satisfied; they seduce the unstable. They are accursed children with hearts trained in greed” (verses 13-14).

“They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness. But he was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice and restrained the prophet’s madness” (verses 15-16).
passages.hearers:
Peter's language is fierce here. Piled-up pictures like these are a style found in the Old Testament prophets and in Jewish moral writing. They are meant to shock readers awake.

Even angels, who are stronger, do not dare to slander such powers before the Lord. But these teachers speak with contempt about things they do not understand. They act on appetite, like animals with no reason.

Worse, they do it inside the church. ‘They feast with you’ refers to the shared meals of early Christian worship, which Jude calls ‘love feasts’. The teachers sat at the church's table, enjoying themselves, while they spread their deception. ‘Blots and blemishes’ are stains on what should be clean.

‘They seduce the unstable.’ The word is the one used for bait. They go after people who are young in faith, lonely, or shaken. And their hearts are ‘trained in greed’, practised in it like an athlete in a sport.

Then Balaam. In the book of Numbers, Balaam was a prophet hired by the king of Moab to curse Israel. He went for the money. On the road, his donkey saw the angel of the LORD and refused to go on, and God opened the donkey's mouth. A dumb animal had more sense than the prophet. Peter's point: these teachers, like Balaam, sell what is holy for money, and an animal could see more clearly than they can.
passages.ot:
Balaam's story is in Numbers 22. “Then the LORD opened the donkey’s mouth, and she said to Balaam, ‘What have I done to you that you have beaten me these three times?’” (Numbers 22:28). “Then the LORD opened Balaam’s eyes, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand” (Numbers 22:31).

Later Scripture remembers him as hired to curse Israel: “they hired Balaam son of Beor from Pethor in Aram-naharaim to curse you” (Deuteronomy 23:4). And it remembers that he led Israel into sin at Peor: “these women caused the sons of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to turn unfaithfully against the LORD at Peor” (Numbers 31:16).
passages.asks: Ask whether there is any part of your faith you would sell, for money, comfort or approval. Ask who in your church is ‘unstable’, young in faith or alone, and whether anyone is looking out for them. And ask whether you have ever been more stubborn than Balaam's donkey.

passages.happening:
“These men are springs without water and mists driven by a storm. Blackest darkness is reserved for them. With lofty but empty words, they appeal to the sensual passions of the flesh and entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error. They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity. For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him” (verses 17-19).

“If indeed they have escaped the corruption of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, only to be entangled and overcome by it again, their final condition is worse than it was at first. It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them. Of them the proverbs are true: ‘A dog returns to its vomit,’ and, ‘A sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud’” (verses 20-22).
passages.hearers:
‘Springs without water.’ In a dry land, a traveller who reached a spring and found it dry was in danger. ‘Mists driven by a storm’ promise rain and give none. These teachers promise much and give nothing.

Their great promise is ‘freedom’. Some Greek thinkers taught that the gods did not judge, so there was nothing to fear in following the body's appetites. The teachers' message sounds the same: no judgment, so you are free. Peter turns it round. ‘A man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.’ Those who promise freedom are themselves slaves to their desires.

And they go after the most vulnerable: people ‘just escaping’ from their old life, newly turned to Christ, still unsteady.

Then a grave warning. To know the way of Christ and then turn back to the old corruption is worse than never knowing it. Peter ends with two proverbs, earthy on purpose: a dog going back to its vomit, a washed pig going back to the mud. Some animals return to what they are.
passages.ot:
The first proverb is from Proverbs: “As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly” (Proverbs 26:11).

Jeremiah used the picture of dry water sources for turning from God: “They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own cisterns— broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

And Ezekiel spoke of the one who turns back: “But if a righteous man turns from his righteousness and practices iniquity, committing the same abominations as the wicked, will he live?” (Ezekiel 18:24).
passages.hard:
Do verses 20 to 22 teach that a true believer can lose salvation?

Christians answer this differently, and these notes do not choose. Arminian and Wesleyan readers take the verses at face value: these teachers had truly escaped the world's corruption through knowing Christ, and then fell away, which shows that real believers can turn back and be lost. Reformed readers hold that the teachers had outward knowledge and a place in the church but were never made new, and they point to the proverbs: the dog and the pig go back to what they always were, never having changed their nature.

Both agree on Peter's warning. To know the way of righteousness and then walk away from it is a terrible thing, and the warning is to be heeded, not only argued about. These verses are about people who deliberately turn back to the corruption they left, and who lead others with them. They are not about a believer who struggles, falls and keeps coming back to Christ.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what promises of freedom you have been tempted by, and what they would make you a slave to. Ask whom you know who is ‘just escaping’ an old life, and how you can stand with them. And ask whether you are holding to the way you have known.
